'''University governance''' concerns how a university directs itself —
the arrangements, rights and responsibilities through which faculty,
administrators and governing boards share authority over academic affairs.<ref name="agb" />
Two principles are central to it: '''institutional autonomy''' and '''academic
freedom'''.

== Institutional autonomy ==

Institutional autonomy is the degree of self-governance and independence a
higher-education institution exercises — free from undue governmental,
commercial or political interference.<ref name="stavros" /> A frequently cited
legal formulation describes it as the university's right to decide, on academic
grounds, who may teach, what is taught, how it is taught, and who is admitted to
study.<ref name="aau" />

== Academic freedom ==

Academic freedom is the recognised principle that gives scholars the autonomy to
pursue intellectual questions within their disciplines, carry out professional
work, and express their views publicly without undue interference.<ref name="mdpi" />
By insulating scholarly work from ideological, political or economic pressure,
it protects the independence and legitimacy of inquiry in service of knowledge
and the public good.<ref name="mdpi2" />

Autonomy and academic freedom are understood to reinforce one another: a
university needs autonomy so that its faculty and students can exercise academic
freedom.<ref name="cambridge" />

== Shared governance ==

A sound system of institutional governance is treated as a necessary condition
for protecting faculty rights and for the productive exercise of academic
freedom.<ref name="aaup" /> The idea that faculty — as professionals in
scholarship and teaching — should be centrally involved in running the
institution is known as '''shared governance'''.<ref name="aaup-sg" />
